extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice/Mayo two-part test), including Step 2B 'significantly more' considerations such as improvements to technology, particular machines/transformations, and conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements to any other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to an improvement in technology (beyond mere computer functionality or abstract ideas) may be patent eligible; such claims should describe how the claimed invention improves the existing technological process rather than merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples: McRO (automatic lip synchronization/facial expression animation) found eligible because claims recited particular rules that automated tasks not previously automatable; Diamond v. Diehr (thermocouple in rubber molding press) is an example of a computer-aided improvement. Examiner guidance: To show a computer assists in improving the technology, claims must recite details regarding how a computer aids the method, the extent of aid, or the significance of the computer. Merely adding generic computer components or instructions to perform the method on generic machinery is insufficient. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for mere-instructions guidance. Examples of improvements the courts found sufficient (included as illustrative): particular computerized rubber molding steps, new telephone/server combinations, improved streaming download processes, improved digital compression, virus screening integration, measurement devices generating new data, specific inertial sensor configurations, structured GUIs that improve accuracy, improved biological preservation processes. Examples of insufficient patents: commonplace business methods on a general-purpose computer (Alice), using standard lab techniques, gathering/analyzing information with conventional techniques and displaying results (TLI), high-level claims to delivering broadcast content to portable devices, generic email screening on a computer, mere selection of content types or generic hardware functions. The improvement must be more than generic application of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine consideration (machine-or-transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the judicial exception is applied with, or by use of, a particular machine; the machine-or-transformation (M-or-T) test is a useful clue but not a standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test first; satisfying M-or-T alone does not guarantee eligibility and failure of M-or-T does not preclude eligibility. If an applicant adds a generic computer or claims a 'specially programmed' machine, examine whether the added machine elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception; merely adding a generic computer/programmed computer does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection. See Bilski, McRO, DDR Holdings, and Alice Corp. citations for context. Examiners may also consider other Step 2B considerations (mere-instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field of use/technological environment) when assessing whether a recited machine provides significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of machine or apparatus elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the degree to which the machine in the claim can be specifically identified (particular) versus generically recited (any and all machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine recited with particular structural details (e.g., specific antenna shape/length/angles in Mackay Radio or a Fourdrinier machine with specific components/arrangement in Eibel) is more likely to provide significantly more. A general-purpose computer that applies an exception by conventional computer functions does not qualify as a particular machine (Ultramercial, TLI). Mere recitation of concrete/tangible components is not necessarily an inventive concept. When applicants assert a 'specially programmed' computer, evaluate whether the claimed elements add significantly more than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the machine implements the steps of the method (integral use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine if the claimed machine plays an integral role in performing the claimed method steps rather than merely being an object on which the method operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine substantially performs or enables the claimed method steps (integral use), it may provide significantly more; if the machine merely hosts or is a medium for the method (i.e., cannot itself perform the claimed steps), it typically does not. Example: CyberSource rejected relying on 'the Internet' as a machine because the Internet could not perform fraud-detection steps. Versata explains that to add significantly more, the machine must play a significant part in permitting performance of the method, not just be an obvious mechanism to achieve a solution faster. See MPEP §2106.05(f) for more on additional elements invoking computers as tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether machine involvement is extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the machine's involvement meaningfully limits the claim or merely contributes nominally (e.g., data gathering, field-of-use restriction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a machine that contributes only nominally or insignificantly (such as mere data gathering or stating the Internet as a source) will not provide significantly more (Bilski, CyberSource, Parker v. Flook). If the machine's recitation only imposes a field-of-use limitation or is extra-solution activity, treat it as not favoring eligibility. See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for additional guidance on insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular transformation consideration (transformation clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claimed process effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; transformation of an article is a clue to patentability but is not a standalone test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim effects a transformation of a particular, identifiable article to a different state or thing (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr, Tilghman v. Proctor), the claim is more likely to be significantly more than a judicial exception. Transformation must be more than mere use or change in location; a new/different function or use is strong evidence. Purely mental processes or manipulation of abstract data (basic mathematical constructs) are not transformations. Consider also other Step 2B considerations (mere-instructions, insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use) when assessing whether the transformation is significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or generality of the transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how particular or definite the transformation is (generalized transformations vs. specific processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (Gottschalk/Benson/Corning) indicate that definite chemical/physical processes (tanning, dyeing, vulcanizing, smelting) that change articles in a specific manner confine the patent monopoly and are more likely to provide significantly more. A more particular, well-defined transformation favors eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which the recited article is particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the transformed 'article' is specifically identified versus generically recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation applied to a generically recited article or 'any and all articles' is less likely to provide significantly more. Transformations that apply only to particular articles or can be specifically identified are more likely to favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the transformation (type/extent of change in state or thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the transformation results in a different function/use for the article rather than merely changing its location or superficial state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A transformation resulting in a different function or use for the transformed article is more likely to provide significantly more; mere relocation or trivial change in state is less likely. Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr) is significant; mere movement is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the article transformed (physical vs intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the transformed item is a physical/tangible object or an intangible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations of physical/tangible objects or substances are more likely to provide significantly more than transformations of intangible concepts (e.g., contractual obligations or mental judgments). Data manipulation (basic mathematical constructs) has not been deemed an eligible transformation (CyberSource quoting In re Warmerdam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the transformation is extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed transformation meaningfully limits execution of the method versus being nominal or peripheral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transformation contributes only nominally or is merely a field-of-use limitation, it will not provide significantly more (Mayo example: administering a drug was deemed only a field-of-use limitation and not significantly more). See MPEP §§2106.05(g) & (h) for further discussion. Consider whether the transformation meaningfully confines the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements (beyond the judicial exception) are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known in the relevant industry; if so, they typically do not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are specific, unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, this favors eligibility (DDR Holdings example: dynamic composite webpage). Conversely, if elements are merely well-known/standard techniques recited at high-level generality (Mayo example: measuring metabolites by any known process), they do not amount to an inventive concept. This consideration overlaps with improvement, mere-instructions, and insignificant extra-solution activity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: A known-in-the-art element can still be unconventional/non-routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether an element known in the art nonetheless represents an unconventional or non-routine application for purposes of Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/obviousness is distinct from eligibility: an element known in the art can still render an invention eligible if it is used in an unconventional way that improves functionality (Enfish example: self-referential database features were considered unconventional despite being anticipated in prior art). Do not conflate prior art novelty with the 'well-understood, routine, conventional' inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search not required to determine conventionality; rely on art/court recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should not generally require a prior art search to conclude an element is well-understood, routine, and conventional; rely on what courts or those skilled in the art would recognize as widely prevalent or common in the industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner should only conclude conventionality when, based on their expertise in the art, the element is readily understood to be widely prevalent or in common use. If the element is not widely prevalent or beyond those elements recognized as conventional in the art or by courts, it will usually favor eligibility. Use examiner expertise and recognized authorities rather than conducting an exhaustive prior-art search for this determination.
